Rates of trait evolution from a history along the tree

Source: R/traits_rates.R
history_rates.Rd

Turns the history of a discrete character along a tree, such as the habitat or region of each lineage from trait_mk() or a stochastic map of phytools, into the rate of evolution of a continuous trait on each branch, for trait_rates(edge_rates = ). The rate is a function of the history at each moment, and the rate of a branch is its mean over the branch, weighted by time. Three models link the history to the rate:

Usage

history_rates(
  history,
  model = c("state", "burst", "sympatry"),
  sigma2 = 1,
  state_rates = NULL,
  burst = 4,
  decay = 0.1,
  r = -0.1,
  overlap = FALSE
)

Arguments

history

A tree with the history of a discrete character, of class simmap, from trait_mk() or phytools.

model

"state", "burst" or "sympatry".

sigma2

Rate before any change of state ("burst") or scale of the rate ("sympatry").

state_rates

For "state", the rate in each state, named by state.

burst, decay

For "burst", the relative increase of the rate at each change of state and the time scale of its decay.

r

For "sympatry", the change in the logarithm of the rate per lineage in the same state.

overlap

For "sympatry", count the lineages whose state shares an area (states such as "A+B", split at "+") rather than those in the same state.

Value

Numeric vector with the rate of each branch, in the order of the rows of history$edge.

Details

  • "state": each state has its own rate, state_rates, as in Brownian motion with several regimes (O'Meara et al. 2006).

  • "burst": each change of state, such as the colonisation of a new habitat or region, multiplies the rate by 1 + burst, and the excess decays exponentially with time scale decay, also along the descending branches, until the next change. The rate at time \(u\) after the last change is \(\mathrm{sigma2}\, (1 + \mathrm{burst}\, e^{-u / \mathrm{decay}})\); before any change it is sigma2. This follows the expectation of McPeek (2017) that selection, and so evolution, is strongest when a lineage first adapts to a new community.

  • "sympatry": the rate depends on the number of lineages that share the state at each moment, counting the lineage itself, as \(\mathrm{sigma2}\, e^{r n}\), with \(n\) that number; a negative \(r\) slows evolution down as lineages accumulate in the same region, as in the diversity-dependent model with biogeography of Drury et al. (2016). With ranges made of several areas, such as those of range_history() ("A+B"), overlap = TRUE counts the lineages whose range shares at least one area with that of the lineage, instead of those with the same range.

References

Drury, J., Clavel, J., Manceau, M., & Morlon, H. (2016). Estimating the effect of competition on trait evolution using maximum likelihood inference. Systematic Biology, 65, 700–710. doi:10.1093/sysbio/syw020

McPeek, M. A. (2017). Evolutionary Community Ecology. Princeton University Press. doi:10.23943/princeton/9780691088778.001.0001

O'Meara, B. C., Ané, C., Sanderson, M. J., & Wainwright, P. C. (2006). Testing for different rates of continuous trait evolution using likelihood. Evolution, 60, 922–933. doi:10.1111/j.0014-3820.2006.tb01171.x

See also

trait_rates(), trait_mk(), as_herodotools()

Other species traits: arrival_ages(), as_herodotools(), food_web_rates(), paint_regimes(), partner_turnover(), plot.rate_matrix(), plot_rates(), plot_traits(), rate_matrix(), region_pool(), species_traits(), tip_history_metrics(), trait_bm(), trait_mk(), trait_ou(), trait_rates(), turnover_rates()

Examples

set.seed(1)
tr <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(30)
habitat <- trait_mk(tr, q = 0.5, states = c("forest", "open"))
rates <- history_rates(habitat, "state", state_rates = c(forest = 1, open = 5))
x <- trait_rates(habitat, edge_rates = rates)
# a burst of evolution after each change of habitat
b <- history_rates(habitat, "burst", burst = 9, decay = 0.1)
summary(b)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   1.000   1.000   1.000   1.393   1.000   5.078 
# slower evolution as lineages accumulate in the same habitat
s <- history_rates(habitat, "sympatry", r = -0.1)
